## Lightning Scheduler: What It Does, and an Alternative (https://multidatepick.com/salesforce-calendar-vs-lightning-scheduler.html)

- Lightning Scheduler is the earlier name of Salesforce Scheduler, Salesforce's appointment scheduling product. It matches a customer to a qualified person at a branch and time.
- Salesforce Scheduler's data model: Service Territory, Work Type Group, Work Type, Service Resource, Service Appointment. Booking runs through Inbound and Outbound flow templates, plus the Inbound New Guest Appointment flow for unauthenticated visitors on an Experience Cloud site.
- Salesforce Scheduler is an extra-cost add-on in Lightning Experience on Enterprise, Performance and Unlimited editions; each service resource needs the Salesforce Scheduler permission set license. Asset Scheduling (rooms and equipment) is a further extra cost. It supports concurrent scheduling and multi-resource appointments with up to five required resources. Source: Salesforce Scheduler Implementation Guide and the Trailhead module Multi-resource, Inbound, and Concurrent Scheduling with Salesforce Scheduler.
- MultiDatePick books appointments, rooms, equipment or people on any standard or custom object, picks many dates, ranges and recurring patterns in one go, shares slots up to a capacity with conflict checks, and shows the same records in seven views (Calendar, Timeline, Week, Utilization, Agenda, Map, Gantt).
- MultiDatePick runs on record pages, App and Home pages, Screen Flows and Experience Cloud sites. Setup is a point-and-click Setup Wizard, no Apex.
- MultiDatePick pricing: one plan, $20 per user per month, every feature, 30-day free trial with no card required, no per-record meter.
- Choose Salesforce Scheduler when customers must be matched to staff by skill and branch territory; choose MultiDatePick for booking and multi-date scheduling on your own objects.
- FAQ covers: what Lightning Scheduler is, Lightning Scheduler vs Salesforce Scheduler naming, whether Scheduler costs extra, Scheduler on Experience Cloud, booking rooms and equipment in Salesforce, a Lightning Scheduler alternative for custom objects, and whether the standard Salesforce calendar is a booking tool.

## Trust & Security | MultiDatePick (https://multidatepick.com/trust.html)

How MultiDatePick handles data and security.

- 100% native Salesforce: no external servers, no outbound callouts, no subprocessors, no telemetry. Data stays in the customer's org.
- Passed the Salesforce AppExchange Security Review.
- Every query that returns data, and every write, runs in USER_MODE and enforces object, field-level security and sharing. Two internal checks run in system mode and return no data: the running user's own permission set count and a row lock before a booking saves. It never elevates privileges.
- Four permission sets: MultiDatePick - Setup (admins, includes the Setup Wizard), MultiDatePick - User (everyone who uses calendars), MultiDatePick - All Access (both), MultiDatePick - Guest (the guest user of a public Experience Cloud site: read and create).
- Saves are additive by default; records are never deleted without an explicit action.
- Keyboard and screen reader support. The VPAT 2.5 at /accessibility.html covers three components and all six views (Calendar, Timeline, Week, Utilization, Agenda and Map) and rates every applicable WCAG 2.1 A and AA criterion as Supports except two, rated Partially Supports: contrast (admins can pick their own status colors) and reflow (the month grid keeps seven columns at 320 pixels wide).
- $20 per user per month, 30-day free trial.

## MultiDatePick for Salesforce Developers and Architects (https://multidatepick.com/salesforce-calendar-developer-guide.html)

Optional, for the times a developer or architect is involved anyway (reviewing the package, building flows around it, moving its setup through sandboxes). Nothing here is needed to set MultiDatePick up.

- What ships: the Dates, Dates & Times and Resource Booking components, the Setup Wizard tab (live preview, JSON import and export), two Flow actions (Parse Date Entries from JSON and Format MultiDatePick Time Range) and four permission sets (MultiDatePick - Setup, MultiDatePick - User, MultiDatePick - All Access, MultiDatePick - Guest).
- Where settings live: every saved setup is a Custom Metadata record. Config__mdt holds the settings and Config_Extension__mdt holds newer ones as JSON in Settings__c. A placement names its config in Config Name; a property also set on the placement overrides the config's text and number values. Configs deploy with change sets, the Salesforce CLI or CI/CD, and move between orgs as JSON.
- Your data stays your data: picks become ordinary records on the objects you choose; no MultiDatePick data model, no external service, no callout. Triggers, flows, validation rules and reports keep working.
- Screen Flow outputs: Selected Dates (text collection, YYYY-MM-DD), Date Ranges JSON, Dates With Times JSON (Dates & Times), Successful Bookings Count (Resource Booking). With Parent Record Id bound the calendar saves its own records; "My flow saves them" in the wizard hands the picks to the flow instead. Resource Booking always saves its own bookings and books nothing with Parent Record Id empty.
- Apex-defined types for looping JSON: MultiDatePickEntryCollection (data, totalCount, success, errorMessage) and MultiDatePickEntry (fromDate, toDate, startTime, endTime, resourceId, resourceName, bookingStatus, relatedRecordId, label).
- Security: every query that returns data and every save runs in user mode (object permissions, field-level security and sharing, guests included); two internal checks run in system mode and return no data. No callouts, servers or subprocessors; passed the Salesforce Security Review.
- Sandbox to production: build and test in a sandbox, deploy the Config__mdt and Config_Extension__mdt records (or export and import the JSON), move the page or flow, assign permission sets.

## Salesforce Flow Loops: Create a Record for Every Date or Shift (https://multidatepick.com/blog/salesforce-flow-loop-multiple-records.html)

Published October 29, 2026. Create multiple records from one Salesforce Screen Flow, with three starter flows to copy.

- The pattern in five elements: a Screen with a MultiDatePick calendar, the Parse Date Entries from JSON action, a Loop, an Assignment that adds each record to a collection, and one Create Records after the loop.
- Why the save goes after the loop: every Create Records is a separate save and Salesforce allows 150 per transaction; a save inside the loop spends one per date (30 dates, 30 saves), a collection saved once spends one and is all or nothing.
- Add Shifts starter flow: pick days and hours; the Dates With Times JSON output is parsed into entries (fromDate, toDate, startTime, endTime); adjacent slots make one shift.
- Record per Day starter flow: loops the Selected Dates text list directly, with DATEVALUE() to turn each item into a date; no parser needed.
- Record per Range starter flow: the Date Ranges JSON output joins adjacent days into one range, so one record per range with a start and end date.
- Resource Booking needs no loop: it saves its own bookings and returns Successful Bookings Count and the dates that clashed.
- The starter flows save to the Schedule and Event objects that come with MultiDatePick; deploy them with VS Code (/deploy-flow-vscode.html), then set Config Name in Flow Builder and point them at your own objects. The no-code alternative: bind Parent Record Id and the calendar saves every record itself.

## Troubleshooting (https://multidatepick.com/troubleshooting.html)

Each MultiDatePick setup message with a screenshot, the cause and a fix: no Save button, Wrong component and Configuration mismatch banners, the red could not load its data banner, Configuration Required, No resources available, Capacity needs both time fields, saved dates not showing, date limit reached, a Flow ignoring Config Name, and site members not seeing records. Access errors: assign MultiDatePick - User (users), MultiDatePick - Setup (admins, includes the Setup Wizard) or MultiDatePick - All Access (both). Insufficient privileges means no Read on the parent object or record; No read access to field means missing Read field-level security (admins too, for new custom fields); Time group failed to save or Insert failed means missing Edit on a field the save writes; INSUFFICIENT_ACCESS_ON_CROSS_REFERENCE_ENTITY means no access to the parent or resource record; guests seeing an empty calendar usually need the sharing rule recalculated, MultiDatePickController class access and an activated site.

## Salesforce VPAT: What Admins Need to Know (https://multidatepick.com/blog/salesforce-vpat-accessibility.html)

Published August 12, 2026, updated October 21, 2026.

- A VPAT is a vendor's self-assessment against accessibility standards, not a certificate.
- It covers WCAG 2.1 A and AA, Revised Section 508 (US public sector) and EN 301 549 (EU public sector).
- Conformance levels: Supports, Partially Supports, Does Not Support, Not Applicable. A few honest Partially Supports entries are a good sign.
- Four questions for a vendor: when was it last verified and against which version; was the packaged version tested; automated, manual or both; is color ever the only signal.
- MultiDatePick's VPAT was verified November 10, 2026 on the unpackaged source and November 7, 2026 against managed package 0.13.0-16, with zero axe-core violations across three components and all six views (Calendar, Timeline, Week, Utilization, Agenda and Map).

### Calendar views
Seven ways to see the same Salesforce records, and when each one fits.

Every room, person or asset down the side, every day across, and each cell showing booked against capacity. Overbooking flags, the combined availability row, and who uses it, from room planning to team capacity.

Rooms, people, equipment or projects down the side, dates across the top, and every booking drawn as one bar. Lanes for overlaps, a capacity strip, Day to Month zoom and drag to reschedule.

Calendar, Timeline, Week, Utilization and Agenda, all reading the same records through the same field mappings, and chosen per placement with one setting. No second install. (A sixth, optional Map view has been added since.)

### Scheduling and booking

## Multiple Dates in a Salesforce Screen Flow (https://multidatepick.com/blog/multiple-dates-in-a-salesforce-screen-flow.html)

How to capture many dates in one Salesforce Flow screen, and what to do with the collection afterwards. Loops, parsing and the limits of standard components.

Flow gives you one Date field per screen element. If someone needs to choose nine days, that is a problem. Here are the options, and the tradeoffs of each.
Every admin hits this eventually. A time-off request, an availability form, a training sign-up: the user needs to select several dates that are not necessarily consecutive, and Flow's standard Date component captures exactly one.

### The workarounds, and why they hurt
The start-and-end workaround is the most common and the most quietly wrong. "I need the 3rd, 4th, 11th and 18th off" becomes 3rd to 18th, which is sixteen days of implied absence. The data looks clean and is simply incorrect.

### The real fix: a screen component that returns a collection
What Flow actually needs is a screen component that lets the user click as many dates as they like and hands back a collection. Once you have that, the rest of the flow is ordinary: loop the collection, create a record per date, done.
MultiDatePick returns several outputs, depending on what you are capturing:

### Turning JSON back into records
Two of those outputs are JSON, because Flow has no native type for "a list of objects with several fields each." You do not parse text in a formula. The package ships a Flow action, Parse Date Entries from JSON, that takes the JSON and returns a proper collection with From Date, To Date, Start Time and End Time. You loop that collection like any other.

### One gotcha that costs people an hour
Want the component to save the records itself? Pass the parent record's Id into Parent Record Id and it creates one child record per date. Leave it blank to loop the output and create the records your own way.

### Decide the record shape before you build
The same nine selected dates can become nine records, or four records if consecutive days collapse into ranges, or one parent record with sub-blocks. Each is correct for a different report. Decide it before you build the flow, because changing it afterwards means migrating data as well as editing the flow.

## Prevent Double Booking in Salesforce: Conflicts & Capacity (https://multidatepick.com/blog/prevent-double-booking-in-salesforce.html)

Validation rules fire after the user has already chosen. How to check availability before selection, and handle capacity where more than one booking fits.

Validation rules cannot see other records. That single limitation is why most Salesforce booking systems discover their conflicts a day late.
Double-booking is a timing problem. By the time anything in standard Salesforce can tell you the room is taken, the user has already chosen it, filled in the rest of the form, and moved on.

### Why the obvious tools do not work
They all share the same shape: reject the user after the choice. Even a correct custom solution produces "that slot is taken, please try again," which is a worse experience than never offering the slot.

### Overlap is not equality
Duplicate rules tempt people, so here is the rule. Two bookings conflict when one starts before the other ends and ends after the other starts. A booking from 9:00 to 10:00 and one from 9:30 to 10:30 overlap by half an hour while sharing no identical field values. Any approach based on matching values will miss it every time.

### Conflict and capacity are different problems
They often get treated as one thing.
- **A conflict**
Two things competing for a resource that holds one. A room, an interviewer, a vehicle.
- **Capacity**
A resource that holds several. The question is how many are left. A class with twenty seats, a shift needing four nurses, a desk zone with sixty spaces.
Treating a capacity resource as a conflict resource means you can never book the second person. Treating a conflict resource as capacity-of-one technically works but loses the counts you probably want to report on.

### Three sensible behaviors
"Block it" is not always right. When somebody selects twelve dates and two of them clash, rejecting the whole submission is hostile. Useful systems offer a choice:
- **Block**
Refuse the save and report the clash. Right when every date matters.
- **Skip**
Save the ten that are free, report the two that were not. Usually the humane default for bulk selection.
- **Allow**
Permit the overlap deliberately. Some businesses overbook on purpose.

### The real fix is earlier
Every mechanism above operates at save time. The fix is to move the check to selection time: query what already exists when the calendar loads, draw it onto the grid, and never offer a slot that is gone. Save-time checks still run as a backstop for the genuine race condition where two people are looking at the same free slot, but they stop being the primary defense.

## Recurring Date Patterns in Salesforce (https://multidatepick.com/blog/recurring-date-patterns-in-salesforce.html)

Every Monday and Thursday for six weeks is a pattern a date range cannot hold. Recurring selection patterns in Salesforce, and how to get them without code.

Every other Tuesday. The 2nd and 4th Friday. The last Saturday of the month. These are ordinary business rules, and Salesforce has no field that expresses any of them.
Recurrence exists in Salesforce for Events and Tasks, and it stops there. The moment your schedule lives on a custom object (a shift, a session, an inspection, an on-call rotation), you are on your own, and the usual answer is that somebody works the dates out on a paper calendar and enters them by hand.

### The two kinds of recurrence people mean
They get conflated, and they need different logic.
Interval recurrence counts forward from a start date and does not care about month boundaries. Occurrence recurrence resets every month, and "last" is awkward because it lands on the 4th or 5th week depending on the month. That single word is where most hand-rolled implementations break.

### Why writing it yourself goes wrong
- **Month lengths vary**
"The 5th Monday" exists in some months and not others.
- **Leap years**
They quietly shift every calculation that assumes a fixed year.
- **"Every other week" needs an anchor**
Every other week starting when? Two people will disagree.
- **Weekends and holidays**
They may need skipping, and your holidays live in your own org data.
- **Generating too far ahead**
It creates thousands of records nobody asked for.
None of these are hard individually. Together they are a week of work and a permanent source of edge-case bugs.

### Generating dates instead of storing a rule
There is a design decision underneath the algorithm: do you store the rule and expand it at read time, or expand it once and store the resulting dates?
Storing dates is almost always the better answer in Salesforce. Concrete date records report, roll up, filter, and drive automation like any other data. A stored rule needs interpreting everywhere it is used, and Salesforce reporting cannot interpret it at all. The tradeoff is that changing the pattern means regenerating, which is why the pattern picker belongs at the point of entry rather than buried in configuration.

### The three patterns, on screen
Custom Day-of-Week comes first, because no standard field expresses it at all. Pick any combination of weekdays, set the interval, give it a range, and the calendar fills in every matching date before you save anything.
Weekdays and Weekends are the two shortcuts people reach for most, and they do the same expansion with one click.

### Let people see the dates before they commit
The best thing a recurrence UI can do is show its work. When the user picks "every 2 weeks on Tuesday" and immediately sees the actual dates highlighted on a calendar, mistakes get caught in the second before saving rather than the week after. It also settles the "every other week starting when" argument instantly, because the anchor is visible.
The same applies to consolidation. If your recurring selection produces Monday to Friday for six weeks, you may want thirty records or you may want six, one per week, with a start and end date. Deciding that at selection time is far cheaper than migrating afterwards.

## Configure a Salesforce Calendar Without Code (https://multidatepick.com/blog/salesforce-calendar-setup-wizard.html)

100+ properties sounds like a project. It is a wizard of four steps that fills in the likely choices for you, with a live preview before you save anything.

Most Salesforce components with real depth make you learn them twice: once to understand the properties, once to remember which combination you picked last time. The Setup Wizard exists so you do neither. It asks where the calendar goes and what each pick should save, fills in the fields it can work out, writes the configuration as metadata, and hands you a name you can use anywhere.

### One way in, plus two shortcuts
The Create New tab opens on the guided setup. Two more tabs sit beside it for configs you already have.
- **The guided setup**
Where the calendar goes, what each pick saves, then the likely fields filled in. Best for most setups.
- **Every setting on one page**
All 100+ settings on one page, with a live preview. Best when you know exactly what you want.
- **Existing Configurations**
Your saved configs with their component type. Open one to edit or clone it.
- **Import**
Paste a config from the Config Library or another org.

### Four steps, start to finish
1. Where it lives: a record page of any object, an app or Home page, a Screen Flow or a public site, and the calendar size.
2. Shape: what each pick saves: one record per day, per range, per time block, one with breaks, or a booking of one resource or several.
3. Jump start: the saved object, with the link, date, title, status, times and resource fields filled in for you. Tabs for rules, closed days, views, hover card, status and every other setting.
4. Review: every section with a Change link and a live preview, then save. The wizard shows the Config Name to paste.

### The shape decides everything
The guided setup asks about the shape of the records you want, rather than about properties. Six cards, each with a small picture of what people pick and what lands in Salesforce:
- One record per day, or per range? Monday through Friday for six weeks can be thirty records or six.
- One record per time block, or one with breaks inside? A training day with a lunch break can be two records or one plus a break.
- Booking a room or person? One at a time, several at once, or add one to a range, a time block or a day with breaks.
You choose that here, on purpose, before any data exists. The shape also picks the right component, so there is nothing else to decide.

### A live preview, before anything is saved
The preview on the Review step renders a working calendar from your choices. Turn on two-month view and it appears. Add status colors and the cells fill. It is the actual component, so what you approve is what you deploy.

### Inside the jump start: Fields, Times, Status
Pick the saved object and the link, date and title are filled in. Every list is filtered to the field types that fit. Times sets the hours people can book, the slot length, the gap after a booking and the notice, and maps the start and end time fields. Status sets a color for each status, the statuses to hide, and the ones people may pick. Other settings holds the Header box: your logo, your name, your band and button colors and a banner photo.

### What it actually writes
Saving deploys a Custom Metadata record. Three things follow:
- It is deployable. Custom Metadata moves through your normal release pipeline, sandbox to production, like any other component.
- It is reusable. Put the name in Config Name on any component and it picks up the whole configuration. One config, many placements.
- It stays in your org. Nothing is stored on a vendor server, so the configuration is yours and it is visible in Setup.
Custom Metadata deploys are asynchronous: the wizard waits about two minutes, then shows the deploy id and a link to Deployment Status if the record has not appeared. Assign MultiDatePick - Setup to admins who build configs.

### Import, export, and the mapping step people miss
The Import / Export tab takes a JSON configuration and turns it into a saved config. That is how the Config Library works: 40+ ready-made configurations covering time-off requests, room booking, hot-desking, interview scheduling, fleet reservation and more.
The step that saves the most time is Smart Field Mapping. Library configs reference the demo objects; your org has its own. The wizard scans every reference the moment you paste, flags each one your org does not have, and puts a dropdown next to it sourced live from the object's real field list. Remap in the wizard, click Apply, and it deploys with the rewritten JSON.
Export works the same way in reverse, which makes configurations shareable. A config that works in one org is a paste away from working in another.

### Using the config once it exists
Drop any of the three components onto a Lightning record page, app page, Home page or Experience Cloud site, set Config Name to the name you chose, and leave every other property blank. The config supplies them. On App, Home and Experience pages, put the parent record in Static Parent Record Id.
The same applies inside a Screen Flow: put the config's name in Config Name and every on/off setting comes from the config. You do not set a single checkbox in Flow Builder; the few flow-only ones (Required, Show Inline, Output Date Ranges as JSON) are off unless you turn them on. Pass the parent record into Parent Record Id.

## Show Only Open Time Slots in Salesforce, No Code (https://multidatepick.com/blog/salesforce-calendar-time-slot-picker.html)

A Salesforce time slot picker: a calendar with bookable slots at any interval, taken times hidden before anyone clicks, live capacity counts, and no code.

Salesforce gives you a date picker and a time field. It does not give you a grid of selectable slots. Here is what a real Salesforce time slot picker takes, and how to get one without building it.
A time slot picker is a specific interface: a calendar where you choose a day, and a grid underneath showing that day broken into bookable intervals, with the taken ones visibly unavailable. Everyone recognizes it, because every booking site on the internet uses it. Salesforce does not ship one.

### What Salesforce actually gives you
A standard Date/Time field renders as a date input plus a time dropdown. It is a form control, and it has no idea what else is booked. Nothing stops a user selecting a slot that is already gone, because the field does not know other records exist. That check happens later, in a validation rule or a flow, after the user has already committed to a choice.
That is the gap. A time slot picker queries existing records before the user chooses, and only offers what is free.

### What a real slot picker has to do

### Why building it yourself is more work than it looks
The rendering is the easy part. These are the parts nobody scopes:
- **Querying bookings**
Efficiently, without blowing governor limits when someone opens a two-month view.
- **Overlap math**
Fiddly the moment bookings can be different lengths.
- **Timezones**
The running user's timezone and the record's are not always the same.
- **Race conditions**
Two people looking at the same free slot at the same moment.
- **Field-level security**
The component has to respect what the running user can see.
- **Accessibility**
A grid of clickable divs is not keyboard navigable by default.
Accessibility needs the most care. A slot grid needs proper ARIA grid semantics, arrow-key navigation, and a state that is conveyed by more than color. It is the part most in-house builds skip, and the part a procurement review asks about.

### Grouping slots so people can actually scan them
A 9-to-5 day at 15 minute intervals is 32 slots. Presented as a flat list, that is a wall. Grouping by period (morning, afternoon, evening) turns it into three short blocks. That helps most when the person choosing is a customer on a phone.

### When you do not need the calendar at all
Sometimes the date is already implied. On a record page for an appointment that already has a date, a month calendar is redundant. Time Grid Only drops the calendar and shows just the slot grid for that one date, taken from a field on the host record or set directly.

### The settings that make the picker
Each one is a field in the Setup Wizard. Nothing here needs code.

### Questions people ask
Q: What is a calendar time slot picker?
A calendar where you choose a day, with a grid underneath that splits the day into bookable intervals. Slots that are already taken are shown as unavailable, so people only pick times that are free.
Q: Does Salesforce have a time slot picker?
Not for your own objects. A standard Date/Time field is a date input plus a time dropdown, and it cannot see other records. MultiDatePick adds a time slot picker that reads existing bookings when the calendar loads and only offers what is free.
Q: Can the time slots be any length?
Yes. The slot interval is any number of minutes. 15, 30 or 60 minutes are typical, and a 45 minute interview slot works the same way.
Q: Do I need Apex or a developer to add a time slot picker?
No. The Setup Wizard writes the configuration, and the component goes on a record page, app page, Experience Cloud site or Screen Flow by setting Config Name. There is no code to write.

## Seven Calendar Views, One Salesforce Component (https://multidatepick.com/blog/salesforce-calendar-views.html)

A month grid cannot answer every scheduling question. Timeline, week, utilization, agenda, map and Gantt views beside it, chosen per page with one setting.

Seven views: Calendar, Timeline, Week, Utilization, Agenda, Map, Gantt (7). Map and Gantt are optional views the admin turns on. Map pins records on a map from the record's or its resource's address, beside a list in date order, and the same map powers a location picker on booking calendars (each branch with its next opening). Gantt draws each record as a bar grouped into phases, with percent done, milestones and links. The post also covers a multi-user calendar (User as the resource: everyone's week on one grid) and has an FAQ.

A month grid is the wrong shape for half the scheduling questions people actually ask. Here is why we added four more views, and how choosing between them became a config field instead of a rebuild.
Every calendar starts as a month grid, because that is what the word makes you picture. Then people start asking questions it cannot answer. "Who is free Thursday afternoon?" "Is Room 4 booked solid next week?" "Which technician is over capacity?" The grid holds all of that data. It just makes you hunt for it.
MultiDatePick renders the same records in seven ways. One component, one set of field mappings, one save path, and a View setting that changes the layout.

### The views, and the question each one answers
Each view is built for one question. Same records underneath, drawn the way that question needs.
- **What is happening on the 14th?**
A month at a time, each day filled with the status of what is booked on it. Days that mix statuses get diagonal stripes. The default, and still the right answer most of the time.
- **Which resource is free, and when?**
Resources down the side, dates across the top. A booking that spans three days draws as one bar, overlapping bookings stack into lanes, and a capacity strip shows how full each day is. Zoom from a single day to a whole month, and drag a bar to move or stretch it. More on the Timeline view.
- **Who is free Thursday at 2pm?**
Seven days across, business hours down, each booking sized to its real length. Bookings that overlap sit side by side in their own status colors, and the strip beside them stays open so you can add one more.
- **Who is over capacity?**
Booked against capacity, per resource per day, on one blue scale. Overbooked days get an orange ring, and a combined row sums the team. Click any cell to drop into that resource's week. More on the utilization heatmap.
- **What is next?**
A flat list of the next 60 days, grouped by date, with the times, statuses and fields you pick. Reads well on a phone and in a shift handover.
Utilization and Agenda are read only by design: they answer a question rather than take a booking. The other four are fully interactive.

### Every view, one definition of a booking
The usual version of this story ends with a second component: its own fields, its own save logic, its own bugs. Here all the views read the same records through the same field mappings, honor the same conflict rules and blocked dates, and write through the same save path. Switching from Calendar to Timeline cannot change what a booking means, because there is only one definition of a booking.
Two settings control it:
- **View**
Which layout the component opens on: Calendar, Timeline, Week, Utilization or Agenda.
- **Available Views**
The views the switcher offers. Leave it blank to offer them all, or narrow it to the two that make sense for this page.
So one component becomes three different tools. A recruiter's Interview Scheduling page opens on Week, because interviews are a time-of-day problem. A facilities manager's Room Booking page opens on Calendar with Timeline and Utilization alongside, because rooms are a capacity problem. A wall display opens on Agenda and offers nothing writable at all.

### Choose the view per placement
An org-wide calendar setting is close to useless, because one company is not asking one question. Sales wants next week. Operations wants next quarter. A shift manager wants today, by the hour. Finance wants a utilization number.
View is set on each placement of the component. Put MultiDatePick on four record pages, a Flow screen, a Home page and a public Experience Cloud site, and each can be a different view of the same objects. No second install, no field mappings to keep in sync.
Timeline has two settings of its own:
When one resource has several overlapping bookings, its row collapses to a single strip with a count, and expands on click into one lane per booking. Density becomes something the user chooses rather than something the data inflicts on them.

### Point the resource lookup at User and it becomes people scheduling
The resource lookup points at any object. Rooms gives you room booking. Equipment gives you checkout. Point it at User and every view above becomes a staffing tool: Timeline is a roster, Week is a shift grid, Utilization is a team capacity dashboard. Managers ask "who is over capacity" about people far more often than about rooms.
There are two ready-made configs for exactly this in the library: Team Capacity Planning, which opens on the Utilization heatmap, and Staff Shift Roster, which opens on Timeline. Both use User as the resource.

### Every config in the library now ships with a view already chosen
Picking a default view is a judgment call, and it is easier to copy one than to make one. So every config in the Config Library now specifies both a default view and a switcher list, chosen for what each config is actually for:
Import any of them, remap the field names to your own schema, and the view choice comes along with it.

## FullCalendar in Salesforce vs MultiDatePick: Which LWC Calendar Is More Customizable? (https://multidatepick.com/blog/fullcalendar-salesforce-lwc-vs-multidatepick.html)

Published 2026-11-01. Feature checklist for a JavaScript calendar library's LWC wrapper and MultiDatePick, with a map from the library's terms to MultiDatePick settings.

- Scorecard over 15 features: MultiDatePick 11 rows won (including Undo of a drag, project plans in a Gantt view, and Busy-only privacy), the library 0, even 4 (drag and drop, event details, labels and buttons, languages and time zones).
- The library customizes through code: an options object, callbacks, and the Salesforce side (Apex to load records, the save, permissions) written by developers. Its timeline and resource views need a commercial license.
- MultiDatePick customizes through settings: 130+ across three components, seven views (Calendar, Timeline, Week, Utilization, Agenda, Map, Gantt), seven ways to save records, booking rules (capacity, conflict checks, minimum notice, booking window, buffers, business hours, blocked days), any standard or custom object, and every query and save as the viewing user.
- Library term map: eventSources (Child Object API Name, Date Field API Name, Rollup Field), background events (Blocked Dates), businessHours (per-resource fields), eventOverlap (Conflict Behavior and capacity), validRange (earliest and latest date, days ahead, minimum notice, buffer), eventDrop/eventResize (timeline drag), resources (Resource Object API Name, including User), slotDuration (Time Interval (Minutes)), locale/timeZone (automatic per user).
- When the library still fits: building a calendar product of your own, a view type no calendar ships, or events outside Salesforce, with developers to maintain it.
- Related: the task-by-task no-code comparison at /blog/no-code-salesforce-calendar.html.

## CalendarAnything vs MultiDatePick: Which Salesforce Calendar Fits Your Team? (https://multidatepick.com/blog/calendaranything-vs-multidatepick.html)

Published 2026-11-02. A viewing calendar compared with a scheduling and booking calendar.

- Scorecard: MultiDatePick 7 rows won, the viewing calendar 1, even 5.
- MultiDatePick builds in multi-date picking, capacity and conflict checks, public booking pages on Experience Cloud and Screen Flow outputs, alongside seven calendar views (Calendar, Timeline, Week, Utilization, Agenda, Map, Gantt). Both have a Gantt view; only MultiDatePick's links tasks, moves the waiting ones when one slips, and shows a critical path, slack and planned dates, and only MultiDatePick has Undo for a drag. The viewing calendar adds Kanban layouts and calendar sync.
- Calendar apps: MultiDatePick offers an Add to Calendar file after each save (Outlook, Google Calendar, Apple Calendar); it does not keep a two-way sync.
- Data: any standard or custom object with a Date or Date/Time field, including Task and Event, and records up to five lookups away with the Rollup Field.

## Avonni Calendar vs MultiDatePick: A Component Library or a Booking Calendar? (https://multidatepick.com/blog/avonni-calendar-vs-multidatepick.html)

Published 2026-11-02. A component library's calendar compared with a finished booking calendar.

- Scorecard: MultiDatePick 7 rows won, the component library's calendar 1, even 5. New rows: project plans (a Gantt view with task dependencies), Undo of a drag and set start times go to MultiDatePick; privacy on public pages is even.
- MultiDatePick builds in capacity and conflict checks, multi-date picking, public booking pages and a utilization heatmap, with no wiring. The wider component library matters if you also want tables, charts and other components.
- No Apex: set up in the Setup Wizard or Lightning App Builder on any standard or custom object; every query and save runs as the viewing user.
- Resource timeline included with every license: rooms, people or equipment down the side, days across, drag to move or resize.
- Screen Flows: add the component to a screen and set Config Name; picked dates, ranges and times come out as Flow variables, or the calendar saves the records itself.

## Privacy Policy: Cookies, Analytics and Forms | MultiDatePick (https://multidatepick.com/privacy.html)

What the multidatepick.com website collects and how visitors control it (the MultiDatePick app itself sends nothing out of the Salesforce org).

- Cookie bar on the first visit with Accept all, Reject all and Settings; three settings: Needed for the site to work (always on, only remembers the choice), Analytics, Where you came from.
- The choice is stored in the browser with a version and date and asked again after 12 months. "Cookie settings" in every page footer reopens it.
- Google Analytics 4 (G-YE5L0ECBSY) runs under Google Consent Mode v2: analytics_storage, ad_storage, ad_user_data and ad_personalization default to denied; only analytics_storage is granted, and only after the visitor accepts. While denied, pages send cookieless pings. The _ga cookies last up to 2 years by default; Google Analytics data retention is set in the account (Google default 2 months, maximum 14).
- First-touch tracking (UTM tags, referrer, landing page, date) is saved in localStorage only after "Where you came from" is accepted, and is sent only with a form. Without it the forms work the same.
- The Notify Me at Launch and Free Custom Config forms send what the visitor types to MultiDatePick's Salesforce org (Web-to-Lead), used to reply and for launch news, not sold.
- Hosted on GitHub Pages; the Test Drive is a Salesforce Experience Cloud site. Each has its own privacy policy.
- Contact: support@multidatepick.com.
